texts.facts: This writ petition is filed challenging Exhibit P6 notice dated 28.7.2017 issued by the 2 nd respondent as also Exhibit P3 test report of the 4th respondent dated 25.11.2016. It is submitted that the 2nd petitioner is the Proprietor of an Oil Mill manufacturing coconut oil. Samples of the coconut oil were collected from the 3rd petitioner's place of business by the 1 st respondent on 3.11.2016. A fine of Rs.15,000/- was imposed on the 3 rd petitioner and a fine of Rs.50,000/- was imposed on the 1 st petitioner. On the ground that the packet did not contain the vegetarian logo, Exhibit P3 report found that the product was misbranded. On 28.4.2018, Exhibit P4 notice requiring the petitioners to attend a hearing before the 2 nd respondent on 19.5.2018 was issued. Though the petitioners attended the said hearing, Exhibit P6 proceedings have been issued. Alleging offence under Section 3(1)(zf)C(ii) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (for short, 'the Act') read with Regulation 2.2.2:4 of the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging & Labeling) Regulations, 2011. It is stated that Exhibit P6, which is seen dated 28.7.2017, was received by the petitioners only on 22.9.2018. It is therefore contended that the proceedings were issued without considering any of the contentions of the petitioners.
texts.arguments: 4. It is contended by learned counsel for the petitioners that the test report which contains a finding that the article is misbranded is completely untenable in law. It is further contended that Exhibit P6 order has been passed without giving the petitioners an opportunity of hearing, since it is dated 28.7.2017. It is stated that there is no power in the Analyst to issue a report in the nature of Exhibit P3 and the reliance placed in Exhibits P6 on Exhibit P3 is completely misconceived. Abraham Son'S Coconut Oil Industries ... vs Food Safety Officer on 12 April, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/137535397/ 2 5. The learned Government Pleader would, on the other hand, contend that the offence of misbranding is clearly made out in the instant case, since the item in question did not contain the vegetarian logo which is imperative in the case of a food article which is vegetarian by its nature. It is stated that the 4 th respondent has all power in terms of Section 46 to consider the question whether the article is misbranded and in case such an offence is made out, the respondents are perfectly justified in issuing an order in the nature of Exhibit P6. It is contended that notice had been issued to the petitioners by Exhibit P4 and the order had been issued after hearing the respondents as well. It is stated that the date shown in Exhibit P6 is only a mistake and that it was rendered on 28.7.2018 and served on the petitioner soon thereafter.
